# Structural Equation Modeling I: Path Analysis and Latent Variables {#sec-sem1}

Structural equation modeling (SEM) is a general framework that includes many of the models in this book as special cases. In this chapter, we first show that familiar analyses (regression, the *t*-test, and ANOVA) can all be written as *path models* in `lavaan`. Then we combine a measurement model, like the CFAs in @sec-cfa, with a regression model to estimate a full SEM.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(lavaan)
library(semPlot)
```

## The data

We return to the ELS:2002 data from @sec-logistic. We keep a small set of variables and give them readable names. `transmute()` creates and keeps only the variables we name.

- `hrsread`: hours per week spent reading outside of school
- `absorbmath`: "Gets totally absorbed in mathematics"
- `absorbread`: "Gets totally absorbed in reading"
- `importmath`: "Mathematics is important"
- `comptest`: standardized math and reading test score
- `ap`: ever took part in an Advanced Placement program (1 = yes, 0 = no)
- `sesq`: SES quartile

The three attitude items are rated from 1 (strongly agree) to 4 (strongly disagree), so we reverse-code them (5 minus the score). Higher values then mean more absorption and importance. As in @sec-logistic, negative values are missing data codes.

```{r}
els <- read_dta("data/ELS_Logistic.dta")

els_clean <- els |>
  zap_labels() |>
  mutate(across(c(bys43, bys87a, bys87e, bys87f, bytxcstd, bys33a, byses1qu),
                ~ if_else(.x < 0, NA, .x))) |>
  transmute(
    hrsread = bys43,
    absorbmath = 5 - bys87a,
    absorbread = 5 - bys87e,
    importmath = 5 - bys87f,
    comptest = bytxcstd,
    ap = bys33a,
    sesq = factor(byses1qu, levels = 1:4,
                  labels = c("Lowest", "Second", "Third", "Highest"))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(comptest))

summary(els_clean)
```

We keep only students with a test score, since it is the outcome in most models below. Many students are still missing one or more predictors.

### Handling missing data

In `lavaan`, `missing = "ml"` uses full information maximum likelihood (FIML), which keeps every case and uses all of the data each case has (see @sec-missing). By default, FIML applies only to the outcome variables. Adding `fixed.x = FALSE` extends it to the predictors. We also use `estimator = "MLR"`, which gives standard errors that are robust to non-normal data. We use these three options throughout the chapter.

## Path analysis

### Simple regression

A path model uses the same `~` operator as `lm()`. The line below regresses the test score on reading absorption:

```{r}
model1 <- 'comptest ~ absorbread'

fit1 <- sem(model1, data = els_clean,
            estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml", fixed.x = FALSE)
summary(fit1, standardized = TRUE)
```

Compare this to the same model fit with `lm()`:

```{r}
lm1 <- lm(comptest ~ absorbread, data = els_clean)
summary(lm1)
nobs(lm1)
```

The coefficients are very close. The key difference is the sample: `lm()` drops every student missing `absorbread`, while the path model keeps all of them. With only one predictor, the standardized coefficient (`Std.all`) is the correlation between the two variables.

```{r}
semPaths(fit1, whatLabels = "std", edge.label.cex = 1.2, sizeMan = 10,
         intercepts = FALSE, nCharNodes = 0)
```

### Independent samples *t*-test

A *t*-test is a regression with one binary predictor. Here, we compare math absorption for students who had and had not taken part in an AP program:

```{r}
model2 <- 'absorbmath ~ ap'

fit2 <- sem(model2, data = els_clean,
            estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml", fixed.x = FALSE)
summary(fit2)
```

The intercept (in the `Intercepts` section) is the mean for students with `ap = 0`. The coefficient for `ap` is the difference between the two group means. AP participants reported slightly more absorption in math.

### One-way ANOVA

A one-way ANOVA is a regression with a set of dummy variables. In `lavaan`, we create the dummies ourselves. We leave out the lowest quartile, which makes it the reference group.

```{r}
els_clean <- els_clean |>
  mutate(
    ses2 = if_else(sesq == "Second", 1, 0),
    ses3 = if_else(sesq == "Third", 1, 0),
    ses4 = if_else(sesq == "Highest", 1, 0)
  )

model3 <- 'importmath ~ ses2 + ses3 + ses4'

fit3 <- sem(model3, data = els_clean,
            estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml", fixed.x = FALSE)
summary(fit3)
```

Each coefficient is the difference in mean math importance between that quartile and the lowest. Because `if_else()` returns `NA` when `sesq` is missing, students with unknown SES stay missing rather than being placed in the reference group by mistake.

### Multiple regression

A multiple regression adds more predictors to the same line:

```{r}
model4 <- '
  comptest ~ hrsread + absorbmath + absorbread + importmath + ap +
             ses2 + ses3 + ses4
'

fit4 <- sem(model4, data = els_clean,
            estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml", fixed.x = FALSE)
summary(fit4, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)
```

All of these models have zero degrees of freedom. Each estimates every possible path among its variables, so it is *just-identified* and fits the data perfectly. That is why there are no fit statistics to interpret. Fit statistics become meaningful once a model places constraints on the data, as the latent variable models below do.

## Identification

Before we add latent variables, we need to know whether a model can be estimated at all. A model is *identified* when there is enough information in the data to estimate every parameter. The information is the number of unique variances and covariances among the observed variables. With *p* variables, there are *p*(*p* + 1)/2 of them. The degrees of freedom equal this number minus the number of parameters estimated.

- **Under-identified** (*df* < 0): more parameters than information. The model cannot be estimated.
- **Just-identified** (*df* = 0): the model can be estimated but fits perfectly, so fit cannot be tested.
- **Over-identified** (*df* > 0): the model can be estimated, and its fit can be tested.

### An under-identified model

A factor measured by only two items is under-identified on its own:

```{r}
#| warning: true
model5 <- 'Read =~ hrsread + absorbread'

fit5 <- sem(model5, data = els_clean, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml")
summary(fit5)
```

The output reports −1 degrees of freedom, and `lavaan` warns that a variance is negative. Two items provide three pieces of information (two variances and one covariance). The model needs four parameters: one free loading, two residual variances, and the factor variance. The estimates it reports cannot be trusted.

### An over-identified model

With four items, there are 10 pieces of information and 8 parameters, so *df* = 2:

```{r}
model6 <- 'Learn =~ hrsread + absorbread + absorbmath + importmath'

fit6 <- sem(model6, data = els_clean, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml")
summary(fit6, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
```

Now fit can be tested, and it is poor (for example, robust CFI = 0.66 and RMSEA = 0.27). The standardized loadings suggest why. The two math items load strongly, but reading hours and reading absorption load weakly. This suggests the four items do not share a single underlying construct. In a real study, we would revisit the measurement model before going further. For this demonstration, we keep it, to show how a measurement model connects to an outcome.

## A full structural equation model

A full SEM has two parts. The *measurement model* links latent variables to their items. The *structural model* specifies the relationships among variables, here a regression of the test score on the latent factor.

```{r}
model7 <- '
  # Measurement model
  Learn =~ hrsread + absorbread + absorbmath + importmath

  # Structural model
  comptest ~ Learn
'

fit7 <- sem(model7, data = els_clean, estimator = "MLR", missing = "ml")
summary(fit7, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)
```

The latent factor is positively related to test scores (standardized coefficient = 0.10), but it explains only about 1% of their variance. The model also inherits the poor fit of its measurement model. A weak measurement model limits what the structural model can tell us, which is why it is good practice to establish the measurement model first.

```{r}
semPaths(fit7, whatLabels = "std", intercepts = FALSE,
         edge.label.cex = 1.1, sizeMan = 8, nCharNodes = 0)
```

@sec-sem2 extends this framework to mediation models, with both observed and latent variables.
